:::{#thm-generalized-inverse-solves}
#### A generalized inverse solves every solvable system

Let $\matr{A}$ be $m \times n$, let $\matr{G}$ be a generalized inverse of $\matr{A}$
(@def-generalized-inverse), and let $\vecf{b} \in \reals^m$.
If $\matr{A} \vecf{x} = \vecf{b}$ has a solution,
then $\matr{G} \vecf{b}$ is a solution.

:::

::: proof

Let $\vecf{x}_0$ be a solution, so $\matr{A} \vecf{x}_0 = \vecf{b}$. Then

$$
\ba
\matr{A}\,(\matr{G} \vecf{b})
&= \matr{A} \matr{G}\,(\matr{A} \vecf{x}_0)
&& \text{(substitute } \vecf{b} = \matr{A} \vecf{x}_0 \text{)}
\\
&= (\matr{A} \matr{G} \matr{A})\,\vecf{x}_0
&& \text{(@thm-matmul-assoc)}
\\
&= \matr{A} \vecf{x}_0
&& \text{(@def-generalized-inverse)}
\\
&= \vecf{b}.
&& \text{(} \vecf{x}_0 \text{ is a solution)}
\ea
$$

:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#exm-generalized-inverse-solves}
#### Solving with a generalized inverse

With $\matr{A} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix}$
and its generalized inverse
$\matr{G} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 5 \\ 7 & 0 \end{bmatrix}$ (@exm-generalized-inverse),
the system $\matr{A} \vecf{x} = (2, 0)$ has the solution $(2, 0)$,
and $\matr{G}\,(2, 0) = (2, 14)$ is a solution too:
$\matr{A}\,(2, 14) = (2, 0)$.
The system $\matr{A} \vecf{x} = (2, 1)$ has no solution,
since the second entry of $\matr{A} \vecf{x}$ is always $0$;
there $\matr{G}\,(2, 1) = (7, 14)$ gives $\matr{A}\,(7, 14) = (7, 0) \ne (2, 1)$.

:::
